3.3

Installing monitoring tools and applying updates

Slides 4-3428.8 min

Competency element 3.3 - proper installation of updates. Sub-lessons 3.3.1 to 3.3.5, videos, real-life example, simulator, animation, flash cards and self-check.

3.3.1  Why installation is a procedure, not a download

1.6 minOpen with the mid-term: yesterday they wrote about choosing tools; today they put one in place. Ask who has ever installed software by clicking 'Next' until it ended.

Yesterday's mid-term closed the first half of Topic 3: you can now describe the categories of monitoring tools and defend a choice with a knock-out list and a weighted matrix. In Class 8 that method selected Wazuh for the Val-des-Pins pilot, with Graylog Open (graylog.org VirusTotal check) as the runner-up. Today we move from a decision on paper to a running system, and that step is where most first deployments fail.

A monitoring tool is different from ordinary software in one important way: it receives a copy of what happens on every system it watches. Logons, file changes, firewall decisions, error messages. If the tool itself is installed carelessly, three things can go wrong at once. The tool may be a tampered copy that sends your data elsewhere. The tool may be configured so that it misses the events you decided to watch in Lab 1. And the tool may consume the disk, memory and processor time of the lab VM (Virtual Machine) until nothing else works, which is exactly the kind of risk that section 6.4 of the Legal Notice asks you to protect against with a snapshot.

That is why competency element 3.3 of the course outline is worded as "proper installation of updates" and why this lesson treats installation as a procedure: a fixed sequence of stages, each with a check, that produces the same result every time it is followed. The word to remember is repeatable. If a colleague can take your written record and rebuild the monitoring server from it, the installation was done properly. If the only trace is your memory of which buttons you clicked, it was not.

1.4 minWalk through Figure 3.3.1 stage by stage; keep the pace brisk, the details come in 3.3.2 to 3.3.4.

Figure 3.3.1 shows the seven stages we will use in Lab 2. Read them once now so that the rest of the lesson has a frame: prepare, obtain, verify, install, check, harden, record. Three of them are shaded because beginners skip them most often: preparing (nobody checks the memory before starting), verifying (nobody compares the checksum of the file they downloaded) and recording (nobody writes down what was done). Each skipped stage removes a safeguard. Skipping all three produces an installation that nobody can trust and nobody can rebuild.

3.3.2  Before installing: requirements, official sources, integrity checks, snapshot, change record

1.8 minShow the sizing table on screen; connect it to MON-01 (8 GB (Gigabyte), 200 GB (Gigabyte)) from Class 8.

Stage one is preparation, and it starts with the system requirements: the minimum processor, memory, disk space and operating system that the publisher states for the tool. Publishers state them because the tool was tested with them. Below them the tool may start, but it will drop events under load or stop when the disk fills. For the Val-des-Pins pilot, the Wazuh documentation gives, for the all-in-one installation that serves 1 to 25 monitored endpoints, 4 virtual processors, 8 gigabytes of memory and 50 gigabytes of disk for 90 days of searchable alerts. The lab server MON-01 defined in Class 8 has 4 vCPU (virtual Central Processing Unit), 8 GB (Gigabyte) of RAM (Random Access Memory) and 200 GB (Gigabyte) of disk, so it passes with room for the 90-day retention that need N-01 requires. Write the comparison down: "required 4 / 8 / 50, available 4 / 8 / 200, pass". That single line is the first row of your installation record.

The OS (Operating System) matters as much as the hardware. A tool is tested on a short list of operating system versions, and MON-01 runs Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS (Long-Term Support) (ubuntu.com/server VirusTotal check), which is on the Wazuh list. An LTS (Long-Term Support) release receives security updates for five years, which is why servers use it: you do not want to re-install the monitoring server because its operating system stopped receiving fixes.

2.2 minThis is the legal and safety heart of the lesson: official source, checksum, snapshot. Slow down.

Stage two is obtaining the software, and here the rule is short: download only from the official source, meaning the publisher's own website or the publisher's own package repository, never from a mirror found through an advertisement, a forum or a video description. Annex C of the Legal Notice repeats this rule for every link in the course, and section 6.6 makes you responsible for the licence of every tool you run. For Wazuh the official site is wazuh.com VirusTotal check and its documentation is at documentation.wazuh.com (Quickstart) VirusTotal check. Note the exact version you download, because "the latest" is not a version: next week "the latest" will be something else and your record will be meaningless.

Stage three is verification of integrity, and it is the stage students are most tempted to skip. A checksum is a fixed-length number computed from the entire content of a file with a hash function; the one used by almost every publisher today is SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit). If a single byte of the file changes, the checksum changes completely, so comparing the checksum you compute on your downloaded file with the checksum the publisher published tells you whether the file is the file. A mismatch does not tell you why: it may be a corrupted download or a tampered copy. In both cases the action is the same: delete the file and download it again from the official source. A digital signature goes one step further: the publisher signs the file or its checksum list with a private key, and you verify the signature with the publisher's public key, typically with GPG (GNU Privacy Guard). A valid signature proves both that the file is unchanged and that it comes from the key holder. Package repositories do this automatically when their signing key is installed, which is why the Wazuh installation assistant imports the repository key before it installs anything.

Two more actions belong to preparation. Take a snapshot of the virtual machine, named with the date and the reason ("MON-01 pre-install 4.14.7"), so that any failure can be undone in one action; this is also a rule of the Legal Notice, section 6.4. And open a change record: a line in your change log that says what will be installed, on which host, when, by whom, and what the way back is. In a company this record is a ticket approved through change management, which you studied in Class 6; in the lab it is a row in your record.

0.5 minRead the definitions once, slowly; students copy them.
Slide 10

Terms to learn

System requirements
The minimum processor, memory, disk and operating system versions the publisher tested the tool with.
Official source
The publisher's own website or package repository; the only place a tool is downloaded from.
Checksum (SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit))
A 64-character hexadecimal number computed from the whole file; any change to the file changes it.
Digital signature
A checksum encrypted with the publisher's private key; verifying it proves origin and integrity at once.
Snapshot
A saved state of a virtual machine that can be restored in one action; taken before every installation and update.
Change record
The written entry that says what is changed, on which host, when, by whom and how it can be undone.

3.3.3  Installing the server and connecting the sources

2.0 minDescribe the three central components without vendor jargon; the point is that one host does three jobs in the lab.

Stage four is the installation itself. Most monitoring platforms are not one program but several cooperating components, and knowing their names helps you read the documentation and the error messages. Wazuh has three central components and one agent. The manager (also called the server) receives events, decodes them, matches them against rules and produces alerts. The indexer stores the alerts and makes them searchable, which is what allows 90 days of history to be queried in seconds. The dashboard is the web interface where you search, look at graphs and manage agents. The agent is the small program installed on a monitored host that reads local logs, checks file integrity and inventories the system, then sends the results to the manager over an encrypted channel. In the lab, all three central components run on MON-01, which the documentation calls an all-in-one installation; in a large organization they would be spread over several servers.

The installation assistant is a single script run with administrator rights on MON-01. It adds the official repository, imports the signing key, installs the three components, generates the certificates they use to talk to each other, starts the services and prints the initial administrator password. The documentation then recommends one action that surprises many students: disable the package repository once the installation is finished, so that an ordinary operating system update cannot upgrade the monitoring platform by accident. We will come back to that in 3.3.5, because it is the difference between an update that happens to you and an update that you apply.

1.8 minTable 3.3.2 is the reference; do not read every row, point at 1514/1515 versus 514.

A server listens on network ports, and a firewall on the server should allow only the ports the connected sources need. Table 3.3.2 lists the ones used in the pilot. An agent first contacts port 1515 over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) to enrol: it presents its name, the manager issues it a unique key, and from then on the agent sends events to port 1514 over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) encrypted with that key. Network devices that cannot run an agent, such as FW-01, SW-01 and NAS-01, send syslog messages instead, usually to port 514 over UDP (User Datagram Protocol); this is the agentless method from the axes of Class 8, and it carries no encryption, which is acceptable inside the isolated lab network and must be reconsidered on a real network. The dashboard is reached on port 443 over HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure), and the server's API (Application Programming Interface) listens on port 55000 for administration tools; in the lab that port is restricted to MON-01 itself, because nobody needs it from elsewhere. Every port you open is written in the record with its reason, so that a reviewer can see that nothing is open without a purpose.

1.8 minConnect this to the Class 7 priority order and the Class 8 gap for CNC-PC-01; Figure 3.3.2 is the visual.

Once the manager is verified, the sources are connected in the order of the Class 7 priority list, because the order encodes what matters most: FW-01 first, then PC-ACCT-01, SW-01, SRV-FILE-01, then CNC-PC-01 and NAS-01. Two hosts receive an agent, PC-ACCT-01 and SRV-FILE-01, which gives us logs, file integrity checks and a software inventory from both. Three devices are connected agentless, by pointing their syslog output at MON-01. One host, CNC-PC-01, receives nothing, because its vendor contract forbids installing software on it; the gap identified in Class 8 stays a gap, and it is written in the record as "no agent, connection records taken from FW-01". A documented gap is a decision. An undocumented gap is a blind spot that someone will discover during an incident. Figure 3.3.2 shows the result.

3.3.4  Checking and hardening a fresh installation

2.0 minAsk: how do you know the installation worked? Push for observable evidence, not 'it said finished'.

Stage five is the check. An installation is verified against observable evidence, not against the message "installation finished". Four pieces of evidence are enough for the lab. First, the services are running: on MON-01 the manager, indexer and dashboard services all report "active". Second, the dashboard answers on port 443 and accepts the administrator login. Third, every enrolled agent shows "active" in the agent list, with the version you installed. Fourth, and this is the one that matters for monitoring, first events arrive: a test logon on PC-ACCT-01 appears in the dashboard within a minute, and a syslog message from FW-01 appears in the search. If the first three pass and the fourth does not, you have a server that runs and monitors nothing, which is worse than no server because it gives false confidence.

Stage six is hardening: making the fresh installation harder to misuse. The generated administrator password is replaced by a strong one stored in a password manager, and the same is done for the internal accounts the assistant creates. A named account with read-only rights is created for the daily checks, following least privilege: the account you use every day should not be able to delete rules or agents. The dashboard's self-signed certificate produces a browser warning; in the lab it is accepted and recorded, and the replacement by a proper certificate is planned as a task before Lab 3. Finally the package repository is disabled, as the documentation recommends, so that the platform version changes only when you decide it. Hardening is documented in the record like every other stage, and the CIS (Center for Internet Security) Benchmarks that Professor Messer mentions in the Secure Baselines video (cisecurity.org/cis-benchmarks VirusTotal check) give a longer list for the operating system underneath.

3.3.5  Applying updates: what, why, in which order, and how to roll back

2.4 minThis is the core of competency element 3.3. Define the three kinds of updates clearly.

A monitoring tool receives three different kinds of updates, and confusing them is a common source of trouble. A software update changes the program itself: the manager, the indexer, the dashboard or the agent. Publishers number these releases; Wazuh uses three numbers, for example 4.14.8, where the first is the major version (large changes, sometimes incompatible), the second the minor version (new features) and the third the patch version (fixes only). This convention is called semantic versioning and is described at semver.org VirusTotal check. A content update changes the detection rules, decoders and lists the tool uses to recognize events, without changing the program; publishers issue these often, sometimes weekly, because attacks change faster than software. The third kind is the operating system update of the monitoring server itself, which is a different product with its own cycle.

Why update at all, if the tool works? Because a monitoring server is a high-value target: it holds copies of everyone's logs and has a network path to every monitored host. A publicly known weakness in it is listed as a CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) entry at cve.org VirusTotal check, scored in the NVD (National Vulnerability Database) at nvd.nist.gov VirusTotal check, and, when attackers are known to use it, added to the CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, United States) KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) catalogue at cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog VirusTotal check. From that moment, an unpatched monitoring server is the easiest door in the building. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security places patching second in its ten priority actions, in publication ITSM.10.096 (cyber.gc.ca, ITSM.10.096 VirusTotal check), and NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology, United States) SP (Special Publication) 800-40 Revision 4 (doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-40r4 VirusTotal check) describes patch management as a planned, recurring activity rather than an emergency. Both documents say the same thing in different words: an organization decides how quickly each kind of update is applied, and then does it on schedule.

2.2 minFigure 3.3.3 on screen. The order manager > agents > content is the exam-worthy fact; say it twice.

How is an update applied safely? The same way the installation was done: as a procedure with checks. Figure 3.3.3 shows the cycle. Watch the publisher's release notes and the advisories that concern your version; a release note tells you whether the release is a patch (fixes only) or a minor version (new features, possibly new requirements). Plan a maintenance window, a period agreed with the system owner when a short interruption is acceptable, and take a snapshot before it opens; for Val-des-Pins the window is Sunday morning, when the workshop is closed. Test the update on a copy first when you have one; in a small organization the snapshot is the test environment, because it can be restored. Apply in a fixed order: the manager first, the agents next, the detection content last. The order is not arbitrary. An agent must never run a newer version than its manager, because the manager may not understand what a newer agent sends; updating the manager first keeps every agent older or equal. Agents can then be updated from the manager itself, which pushes a signed package to each one and restarts it. Content is refreshed last, once the software is stable, and the restart it requires is tested. Verify each component against a stated expectation, exactly as after the installation: version, status, and events still arriving. Record the result.

1.6 minRollback: define it, then link to snapshots and to the PC-ACCT-01 failure in the example that follows.

When a verification fails, the answer is rollback: return the component to the state it had before the change. For the whole server that means restoring the snapshot taken at the start of the window; for one agent it means re-installing the previous agent package. Rollback is done immediately, before the next host is touched, and the failure is written down with a ticket so that the cause is found later, calmly. Notice the logic: a rollback is possible only because the snapshot exists and because the previous package version is known, which is why both were written in the record before the window opened. The two rules in Figure 3.3.3 summarize the lesson: no agent newer than its manager, and no change without a tested way back.

Finally, the cadence: how often each kind of update is applied. A reasonable schedule for a small organization is written in Table 3.3.4 and becomes part of the Lab 2 record: operating system security updates automatically within a week, platform patch releases in the next monthly window, minor versions after a test in the lab, and detection content weekly or automatically, because it changes nothing in the program. The schedule is the answer to the question an auditor asks first: "when was this last updated, and when will it be next?"

Real-life example 3.3 - Installing the pilot on MON-01 and applying the first patch

Task
Install the Wazuh manager on MON-01, connect the six Val-des-Pins sources in the Class 7 order, harden the server, and one week later apply the patch 4.14.7 to 4.14.8 in a maintenance window, with verification and rollback. Produce the Installation and Update Record.
Relation to the lecture
This is Lesson 3.3 applied to the fictional organization used since Class 6: the seven stages of Figure 3.3.1, the ports of Table 3.3.2, the checks of Table 3.3.3 and the update order of Figure 3.3.3, executed on the server selected in Class 8 for the sources prioritized in Class 7.
Deliverable
The Installation and Update Record (Table 3.3.5 below, CSV (Comma-Separated Values)) is Section 4 of the Lab 2 documentation. Lab 2 (Saturday, October 3) starts with exactly these stages on your lab VM (Virtual Machine); Lab 3 (October 16) reuses the record when it proposes optimizations.

It is Saturday, October 3, 2026, 14:05, and the Lab 2 session has started. Your lab virtual machine MON-01 runs Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS (Long-Term Support) with 4 vCPU (virtual Central Processing Unit), 8 GB (Gigabyte) of RAM (Random Access Memory) and 200 GB (Gigabyte) of disk. You compare it with the vendor's table (4 / 8 / 50 for up to 25 endpoints): it passes. You take the snapshot "MON-01 pre-install 4.14.7" in VirtualBox (virtualbox.org VirusTotal check). You download the installation assistant from the official documentation page and compute its SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) checksum. The first comparison in the simulation below is deliberately made against a tampered copy, one byte longer than the original, so that you can see what a mismatch looks like: the two 64-character values differ from the first characters. The genuine file matches, and only then do you run the assistant with administrator rights.

Twenty minutes later the three services report "active", you open the dashboard on port 443, accept the self-signed certificate warning (and write that down), and log in. You add five firewall rules on MON-01, one per port of Table 3.3.2, each with its reason. You verify the manager version, then connect the sources in the Class 7 order. FW-01, SW-01 and NAS-01 are pointed at MON-01 over syslog and their first messages appear in the search. PC-ACCT-01 and SRV-FILE-01 each receive an agent: the agent enrols on port 1515, obtains its key and starts sending on port 1514; both show "active 4.14.7" in the agent list. CNC-PC-01 is recorded as a documented gap. You harden: new passwords, a named read-only account for the daily checks, the certificate status recorded, the repository disabled. The record now has 23 rows.

One week later, Sunday, October 11, 09:00, in the window agreed with the owner, you read the release notes for 4.14.8: a patch release, fixes only. You take the snapshot "MON-01 pre-update 4.14.8", update the central components, and verify that MON-01 reports 4.14.8 with all services running. You push the signed agent package to PC-ACCT-01 from the manager. The verification fails: the agent still reports 4.14.7 and shows "disconnected" for more than five minutes. You roll PC-ACCT-01 back to 4.14.7 by re-installing the previous package, confirm it is active again, and open ticket 2026-0411 to find the cause later. You push the package to SRV-FILE-01: it verifies at 4.14.8. You update the rules and decoders last and test the restart. The record closes at 33 rows: what was done, when, by whom, with which result. That file is what Lab 2 asks you to hand in.

Code example 3.3 - Installation and update simulator (Python program, mirrored step by step in the page)

Task
The program simulates the seven installation stages and the update cycle of the real-life example, produces the same trace you see in the window, and writes the Installation and Update Record as a CSV (Comma-Separated Values) file. Nothing real is installed: it is the procedure that is being practised.
Relation to the lecture
Each function is one stage of Lesson 3.3: check_requirements (3.3.2), snapshot (3.3.2), verify_download (3.3.2, SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit)), install_manager and open_ports (3.3.3), connect_sources (3.3.3), harden (3.3.4), verify and rollback (3.3.4 and 3.3.5), apply_update (3.3.5, manager first, agents next, rules last). The visualization shows MON-01 and its sources changing state as each step runs.
Program
class11_install_update.py (245 lines, a comment line before every code line; Python 3, standard library only) - mirrored step by step by class11_install_update_simulator.js in this page.
Step 0 / ? - ready
1# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
2# class11_install_update.py
3# Cyber.SoHo / Asen Grozdanov - 420-1C1-DW Preventative Monitoring - Class 11
4# Lesson 3.3 - Installing monitoring tools and applying updates
5#
6# TASK: Simulate, step by step, the controlled installation of the Wazuh
7# manager on the monitoring server MON-01 of Ebenisterie Val-des-Pins Inc.,
8# the connection of the monitored sources chosen in Lab 1 and Class 8, and a
9# controlled patch update (4.14.7 -> 4.14.8) with verification and rollback.
10# Every action is written to an "Installation and Update Record" CSV file,
11# which is the Lab 2 deliverable that Lesson 3.3 prepares.
12#
13# RELATION TO THE LECTURE: each function is one stage of the 3.3 procedure
14# (check requirements, snapshot, verify the download, install, open ports,
15# enrol sources, harden, update, verify, roll back, record). Run it in your
16# lab virtual machine only. It touches no real system: everything is simulated.
17# Legal Notice, Terms of Use and Acceptable Use Policy (v2.0) applies:
18# https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.html
19# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

21# The hashlib module gives us SHA-256, the checksum used to verify a download.
22import hashlib
23# The csv module writes the installation record as a spreadsheet-readable file.
24import csv
25# datetime and timedelta build the simulated timestamps of each recorded step.
26from datetime import datetime, timedelta
27
28# Description of the monitoring server as it exists in the lab (Class 8: MON-01).
29SERVER = {"host": "MON-01", "os": "Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS", "vcpu": 4, "ram_gb": 8, "disk_gb": 200}
30# Minimum hardware published by the vendor for 1 to 25 agents (Wazuh quickstart, Sept. 2026).
31REQUIREMENTS = {"vcpu": 4, "ram_gb": 8, "disk_gb": 50}
32# The version we install today and the patch version we update to later in the program.
33INSTALL_VERSION, UPDATE_VERSION = "4.14.7", "4.14.8"
34# The sources to connect, in the priority order decided in Class 7, with their connection method.
35SOURCES = [
36 # The firewall cannot run an agent; it sends its logs by syslog (agentless).
37 {"host": "FW-01", "method": "syslog", "tier": 1},
38 # The accounting workstation gets an agent (endpoint monitoring, category C5).
39 {"host": "PC-ACCT-01", "method": "agent", "tier": 1},
40 # The core switch sends syslog messages (agentless).
41 {"host": "SW-01", "method": "syslog", "tier": 1},
42 # The file server gets an agent (logs, file integrity, inventory).
43 {"host": "SRV-FILE-01", "method": "agent", "tier": 1},
44 # The CNC computer is under a no-software vendor contract: no agent, only FW-01 connection records.
45 {"host": "CNC-PC-01", "method": "none", "tier": 2},
46 # The backup NAS sends syslog messages (included by documented override in Class 7).
47 {"host": "NAS-01", "method": "syslog", "tier": 3},
48]
49# The network ports the monitoring server must accept, with the protocol and the reason.
50PORTS = [
51 (1514, "TCP", "agent events (encrypted channel)"),
52 (1515, "TCP", "agent enrolment (registration)"),
53 (514, "UDP", "syslog from FW-01, SW-01 and NAS-01"),
54 (443, "TCP", "web dashboard over HTTPS"),
55 (55000, "TCP", "server API, restricted to MON-01 itself"),
56]
57# A simulated installer file: in the lab this is the real file you download from the official site.
58DOWNLOADED_FILE = b"wazuh-install.sh version 4.14.7 (simulated official package)"
59# The checksum "published" by the vendor for that file; here it is computed from the same content.
60PUBLISHED_SHA256 = hashlib.sha256(DOWNLOADED_FILE).hexdigest()
61# A tampered copy, used later to show what a failed checksum comparison looks like.
62TAMPERED_FILE = b"wazuh-install.sh version 4.14.7 (simulated official package) + one extra byte"
63
64# The list that becomes the Installation and Update Record CSV file.
65RECORD = []
66# The simulated clock starts at the beginning of the Lab 2 installation window.
67CLOCK = datetime(2026, 10, 3, 14, 5)
68# A counter that numbers every recorded step.
69STEP = 0
70
71
72# One helper function writes a trace line on screen and a row in the record.
73def log(phase, component, action, result, version="", note=""):
74 # We change the global counter and clock, so we declare them global here.
75 global STEP, CLOCK
76 # Each call is one more step.
77 STEP += 1
78 # Each step is assumed to take three minutes on the simulated clock.
79 CLOCK += timedelta(minutes=3)
80 # A row is appended to the record: this is what Lab 2 asks you to hand in.
81 RECORD.append([STEP, CLOCK.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M"), phase, component, action, result, version, note])
82 # The same information is printed as the trace the class discusses step by step.
83 print(f"[{STEP:02d}] {CLOCK:%H:%M} {phase:<8} {component:<12} {action:<34} -> {result} {version} {note}")
84
85
86# Stage 1: compare the server with the vendor requirements before touching anything.
87def check_requirements():
88 # Start by assuming the server passes.
89 ok = True
90 # Look at each requirement one by one.
91 for key, needed in REQUIREMENTS.items():
92 # Read what the server actually has.
93 actual = SERVER[key]
94 # The check passes when the server offers at least the required amount.
95 passed = actual >= needed
96 # Remember a single failure: one missing resource blocks the installation.
97 ok = ok and passed
98 # Record the comparison so the reader can see the numbers.
99 log("prepare", SERVER["host"], f"check {key}", "pass" if passed else "FAIL", "", f"{actual} vs {needed} required")
100 # The caller decides what to do with the result.
101 return ok
102
103
104# Stage 2: take a virtual machine snapshot so the whole change can be undone.
105def snapshot(name):
106 # In VirtualBox this is the "Take snapshot" action; here it is recorded only.
107 log("prepare", SERVER["host"], "take VM snapshot", "done", "", name)
108
109
110# Stage 3: verify the downloaded file against the published checksum.
111def verify_download(data, published):
112 # Compute the SHA-256 of the file we actually have.
113 computed = hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()
114 # Compare with the value published on the official site.
115 match = computed == published
116 # Record both values (shortened) so the class can compare them visually.
117 log("obtain", "installer", "compare SHA-256", "match" if match else "MISMATCH", "", f"computed {computed[:12]}... published {published[:12]}...")
118 # A mismatch means the file must be deleted and downloaded again, never installed.
119 return match
120
121
122# Stage 4: install the manager (server, indexer and dashboard on one host).
123def install_manager(version):
124 # The official installation assistant is the command run in the lab.
125 log("install", SERVER["host"], "run installation assistant", "installed", version, "server + indexer + dashboard")
126 # The services are started and their status is checked.
127 log("install", SERVER["host"], "start services", "running", version, "wazuh-manager, wazuh-indexer, wazuh-dashboard")
128
129
130# Stage 5: open only the ports the connected sources need.
131def open_ports():
132 # Every port in the list becomes one firewall rule on MON-01.
133 for port, proto, why in PORTS:
134 # Each rule is recorded with its reason, which is what an auditor asks for.
135 log("install", SERVER["host"], f"allow {port}/{proto}", "rule added", "", why)
136
137
138# Stage 6: connect each monitored source according to its method.
139def connect_sources(version):
140 # Go through the sources in priority order.
141 for src in SOURCES:
142 # An agent is installed on the host and enrolled with the manager.
143 if src["method"] == "agent":
144 log("connect", src["host"], "install and enrol agent", "active", version, "key issued by MON-01, port 1515 then 1514")
145 # A network device is configured to send syslog messages to MON-01.
146 elif src["method"] == "syslog":
147 log("connect", src["host"], "point syslog to MON-01", "receiving", "", "514/UDP, first message seen")
148 # A host that cannot receive software is documented as a gap, not silently skipped.
149 else:
150 log("connect", src["host"], "no agent (vendor contract)", "gap noted", "", "connection records come from FW-01")
151
152
153# Stage 7: harden the fresh installation before it is left running.
154def harden():
155 # The generated administrator password is replaced by one kept in the password manager.
156 log("harden", SERVER["host"], "change default passwords", "done", "", "admin and API users")
157 # A named account is created for each student so actions can be attributed.
158 log("harden", SERVER["host"], "create named read-only account", "done", "", "least privilege for daily checks")
159 # The dashboard certificate warning is documented and a proper certificate is planned.
160 log("harden", SERVER["host"], "record certificate status", "self-signed", "", "replacement planned before Lab 3")
161
162
163# Stage 8: verify a component after an install or an update.
164def verify(component, expected, observed):
165 # The component passes when the observed version equals the expected one.
166 ok = observed == expected
167 # Record the outcome; a failure will trigger a rollback.
168 log("verify", component, "check version and status", "pass" if ok else "FAIL", observed, f"expected {expected}")
169 # The caller uses the result to decide the next action.
170 return ok
171
172
173# Stage 9: undo a change on one component.
174def rollback(component, previous):
175 # Rolling back means restoring the previous version or snapshot, then re-checking.
176 log("rollback", component, "restore previous version", "restored", previous, "ticket opened, retry after root cause")
177
178
179# Stage 10: the controlled update, in the order manager first, agents next, rules last.
180def apply_update(old, new):
181 # The clock is a global value, so we declare it before changing it.
182 global CLOCK
183 # The update happens one week later, in the agreed maintenance window (Sunday morning).
184 CLOCK = datetime(2026, 10, 11, 8, 57)
185 # Reading the release notes is the first action of any update.
186 log("update", "release notes", f"read notes {old} -> {new}", "reviewed", new, "patch release: fixes only")
187 # A snapshot before the update gives us a way back.
188 snapshot("MON-01 pre-update " + new)
189 # The manager is always updated first: agents must never be newer than the manager.
190 log("update", SERVER["host"], "update central components", "updated", new, "maintenance window 2026-10-11 09:00")
191 # The manager is verified before any agent is touched.
192 verify(SERVER["host"], new, new)
193 # Each agent is updated and verified one at a time.
194 for src in [s for s in SOURCES if s["method"] == "agent"]:
195 # The update is pushed from the manager (remote upgrade with a signed package).
196 log("update", src["host"], "push agent update", "sent", new, "signed package from MON-01")
197 # In this simulation PC-ACCT-01 fails its check: it reports the old version and disconnects.
198 observed = old if src["host"] == "PC-ACCT-01" else new
199 # A failed verification is rolled back immediately, before moving on.
200 if not verify(src["host"], new, observed):
201 rollback(src["host"], old)
202 # Detection rules and decoders are refreshed last, after the software is stable.
203 log("update", SERVER["host"], "update ruleset and decoders", "updated", "", "content update, restart tested")
204
205
206# The main sequence ties the stages together in the order taught in Lesson 3.3.
207def main():
208 # Nothing is installed if the server is too small; the record shows why.
209 if not check_requirements():
210 # The program stops here in that case.
211 return
212 # The pre-installation snapshot protects the lab VM.
213 snapshot("MON-01 pre-install " + INSTALL_VERSION)
214 # First we show what a tampered file looks like: the checksum does not match.
215 verify_download(TAMPERED_FILE, PUBLISHED_SHA256)
216 # Then the genuine file is verified and the installation may proceed.
217 if verify_download(DOWNLOADED_FILE, PUBLISHED_SHA256):
218 # The manager is installed on MON-01.
219 install_manager(INSTALL_VERSION)
220 # The needed ports are opened.
221 open_ports()
222 # The installation is verified before anything is connected to it.
223 verify(SERVER["host"], INSTALL_VERSION, INSTALL_VERSION)
224 # The sources are connected in priority order.
225 connect_sources(INSTALL_VERSION)
226 # The installation is hardened.
227 harden()
228 # One week later the patch update is applied in a maintenance window.
229 apply_update(INSTALL_VERSION, UPDATE_VERSION)
230 # Finally the record is written to a CSV file for the Lab 2 submission.
231 with open("Table_3.3.5_Installation_and_Update_Record.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
232 # A writer object formats the rows as comma-separated values.
233 w = csv.writer(f)
234 # The header row names the columns of the record.
235 w.writerow(["No", "Timestamp", "Phase", "Component", "Action", "Result", "Version", "Note"])
236 # Every recorded step becomes one row.
237 w.writerows(RECORD)
238 # A closing message tells the user where the record is.
239 print(f"\nRecord written: {len(RECORD)} rows -> Table_3.3.5_Installation_and_Update_Record.csv")
240
241
242# Standard Python entry point: run main() only when the file is executed directly.
243if __name__ == "__main__":
244 # Start the simulation.
245 main()
Download

Step-by-step explanation

  1. The program starts by describing the server (MON-01) and the vendor's minimum requirements as two small tables, then compares them value by value. One failed comparison ends the program: nothing is installed on a server that is too small.
  2. A snapshot is recorded with a name that says which host, which moment and which version. In the lab this is the VirtualBox 'Take snapshot' action; the program only records it, because a program cannot know whether you really took it.
  3. The download is verified twice on purpose. The first time the program hashes a tampered copy of the installer and prints 'MISMATCH' next to the two checksums; the second time it hashes the genuine file and prints 'match'. The hashing function is SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) from Python's standard library, the same function you run by hand in the lab.
  4. The installation stage records the assistant run and the three services. The port stage writes one rule per port with its reason, so the record answers 'why is this open?' for every port.
  5. The sources are connected in the Class 7 order, and the program chooses the action from each host's method: agents enrol and become 'active', syslog devices start 'receiving', and the host with no agent is written as a 'gap noted' row instead of being skipped silently.
  6. Hardening writes three rows: password change, named read-only account, certificate status. Then the update function jumps the simulated clock to the maintenance window, reads the release notes, takes a new snapshot, updates the manager and verifies it before any agent is touched.
  7. During the agent updates, the program makes PC-ACCT-01 report the old version, which makes its verification fail. The program rolls that agent back at once and continues with SRV-FILE-01, then updates the detection content last. Every step is appended to the record.
  8. At the end the record is written to a CSV (Comma-Separated Values) file with a header row. Open it in a spreadsheet: it is the Lab 2 deliverable in its final form, and the same rows appear in the trace window of the simulator.

Flash cards (click to flip)

Card 1What are the seven stages of a proper installation, in order?click to flip
Answer 1Prepare, obtain, verify, install, check, harden, record. Preparing, verifying and recording are the three most often skipped.click to flip back
Card 2What does a matching SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) checksum prove, and what does a mismatch tell you to do?click to flip
Answer 2It proves the downloaded file is byte-for-byte the file the publisher published. A mismatch means: delete the file and download it again from the official source; never install it.click to flip back
Card 3In which order are the parts of a monitoring platform updated, and why?click to flip
Answer 3Manager first, agents next, detection content last. An agent must never be newer than its manager, because the manager may not understand what a newer agent sends.click to flip back
Card 4Name the three kinds of updates a monitoring tool receives.click to flip
Answer 4Software updates (major, minor, patch versions of the program), content updates (rules, decoders, lists), and operating system updates of the server that hosts it.click to flip back
Card 5What must exist before any update is applied, and what is done when verification fails?click to flip
Answer 5A tested way back: a snapshot or the previous package. When verification fails, the component is rolled back immediately, a ticket is opened, and the cause is found later.click to flip back

Slides 32-34

Self-check: 4 multiple-choice and 2 multiple-select questions

MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question): one correct option out of four. MSQ (Multiple-Select Question): six options, the number of correct ones is stated. Each question has a hint, a check, and an explanation for every option.

MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) - one answerQ1. MON-01 has 4 vCPU (virtual Central Processing Unit), 8 GB (Gigabyte) of RAM (Random Access Memory) and 200 GB (Gigabyte) of disk. The vendor's table for 1 to 25 endpoints asks for 4 vCPU (virtual Central Processing Unit), 8 GB (Gigabyte) and 50 GB (Gigabyte). What is the correct first row of the installation record?
Hint: Compare each value with 'at least' in mind, and remember that the record is written before anything is installed.
A"Required 4 / 8 / 50, available 4 / 8 / 200, pass" - proceed to the snapshot.
Correct. Every value is at least the required value, so the server passes; the comparison itself is the first recorded step.
B"Disk oversized" - reduce the virtual disk to 50 GB (Gigabyte) before installing.
Extra disk is never a reason to fail; the 200 GB (Gigabyte) serves the 90-day retention of need N-01.
C"RAM (Random Access Memory) equal to the minimum" - fail, add memory before installing.
Equal to the minimum is a pass; the requirement is 'at least'.
DNo row is needed: requirements are checked only after the installation.
Requirements are checked before installation, not after; installing on a server that is too small wastes the window and can damage the lab VM (Virtual Machine).
MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) - one answerQ2. You download the installation file from the official site and compute its SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit). The value differs from the one published on the site. What do you do?
Hint: A checksum comparison has only two outcomes, and one of them has only one acceptable action.
AInstall anyway; small differences are normal after a download.
A mismatch means the file is not the file; installing it can put a tampered program on the monitoring server.
BDelete the file and download it again from the official source; install only when the values match.
Correct. Corrupted or tampered, the action is the same: get the file again and compare again.
CChange the published value in your record to match the computed one.
The published value is the reference; editing it removes the only protection the check provides.
DRun the installer with administrator rights so that the checksum is recomputed.
Administrator rights do not change the content of the file, and running an unverified installer with them is the most dangerous option.
MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) - one answerQ3. During the update window the manager is at 4.14.8 and you are about to update the agents. Which statement is correct?
Hint: Think about who must understand whom.
AAgents may be updated before the manager as long as they are restarted.
An agent newer than its manager can send data the manager does not understand; the order manager first prevents that.
BAgents must never run a version newer than the manager, so the manager is updated first and the agents follow.
Correct. This is the fixed order of Figure 3.3.3: manager, agents, then detection content.
COnly the dashboard needs to be updated; agents update themselves automatically at every restart.
The dashboard is one of three central components, and agents are updated deliberately, from the manager, with a signed package.
DAgents are updated by re-installing the operating system of each host.
An agent update replaces the agent package only; the operating system is untouched.
MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) - one answerQ4. Which piece of evidence shows that the installation monitors something, rather than merely running?
Hint: Three of the checks concern the server itself; one concerns the data.
AThe three services report 'active'.
Running services prove the server is up, not that events arrive.
BThe dashboard accepts the administrator login on port 443.
A working login proves the dashboard works, not that sources are connected.
CA test logon on PC-ACCT-01 appears in the dashboard within a minute.
Correct. First events arriving is the check that the monitoring chain works end to end.
DThe installer printed 'Installation finished'.
A printed message is not evidence; the check is made against observable results.
MSQ (Multiple-Select Question) - select 3Q5. Which three actions belong to the preparation stage, before any installation starts? (select 3)
Hint: Preparation is everything that happens before the installer runs.
ACompare the server with the published system requirements.
Correct: requirements are checked first.
BTake a named snapshot of the virtual machine.
Correct: the snapshot is the way back.
CChange the default administrator password.
This is hardening, after the installation.
DOpen a change record that says what, where, when, who and the way back.
Correct: the change record opens before the change.
EUpdate the detection rules and decoders.
Content updates come last in the update cycle, after the software is stable.
FCreate a named read-only account for daily checks.
This is hardening, after the installation.
MSQ (Multiple-Select Question) - select 3Q6. PC-ACCT-01 fails verification after its agent update (it reports 4.14.7 and shows 'disconnected'). Which three actions are part of the correct response? (select 3)
Hint: Rollback is immediate; investigation is later; the other hosts are not held hostage.
ARoll PC-ACCT-01 back to 4.14.7 by re-installing the previous package.
Correct: the failed component returns to its previous state at once.
BOpen a ticket so the cause is found after the window.
Correct: the record and the ticket keep the failure visible.
CRoll the manager back to 4.14.7 as well, to keep everything equal.
The manager passed its verification; a manager newer than an agent is allowed, the reverse is not.
DContinue with SRV-FILE-01: one failure does not stop the verification of the others.
Correct: each host is verified on its own.
EDelete the snapshot, since the manager update succeeded.
The snapshot is kept until the whole window is verified; it is the way back for the server.
FUpdate the detection content first, then retry the agent.
Content is updated last, once the software is stable; retrying the agent comes after the cause is known.
3.4

Creating the reference database (baseline of normal activity)

Slides 35-6025 min

Competency element 3.4 - efficient creation of the reference database. Sub-lessons 3.4.1 to 3.4.5, videos, real-life example, simulator, animation, flash cards and self-check.

3.4.1  What a reference database is, and why detection depends on it

1.8 minStart from a question: 'Is 35 logons at 22:00 a problem?' Let them answer 'it depends' and ask on what.

The tool installed in 3.3 now receives a copy of everything: every logon on SRV-FILE-01, every decision of FW-01, every change to a watched file. The next question is the one that every detection system must answer before it can raise an alarm: what is normal here? Thirty-five logons on the file server at ten in the evening are alarming in a woodworking shop that closes at five, and unremarkable in a hospital. A monitoring tool cannot know which one it is installed in. Somebody has to measure it and write it down. That written measurement is the reference database, called the baseline in most tools and in the course outline; the two words mean the same thing and we will use both.

A baseline is a documented description of the normal activity of a system, a network or an account, measured over a representative period and stored with enough detail to compare new activity against it. The comparison is the basis of anomaly-based detection, which the course outline reaches in Topic 5: an anomaly is activity that departs from the baseline by more than an agreed margin. Without a baseline there is no margin, so every alert is either a signature match (something known and bad) or a guess. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology, United States) SP (Special Publication) 800-94 (doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-94 VirusTotal check) describes anomaly-based detection exactly this way: the system builds profiles of normal behaviour over a training period and flags significant deviations; NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology, United States) SP (Special Publication) 800-92 (doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-92 VirusTotal check) adds that log analysis is only as good as the understanding of what the logs normally contain.

1.4 minMake the link to competency element 3.4 ('efficient creation of the reference database') and to Topic 6.1 (updating it).

Competency element 3.4 asks for the "efficient creation of the reference database", and competency element 5.1, which we reach in Class 17, asks for its "comprehensive update". The two belong together: a baseline is created once, then maintained, because networks change. A new employee, a new server, a new backup schedule all move the line of normal. A baseline that is not reviewed drifts away from reality in both directions: it starts raising alarms about activity that is now ordinary, and it stops noticing activity that is now suspicious because the margin was set for a busier time. So the Baseline Record you will build in Lab 2 carries a version number, a date and a review date from the day it is created. The review date for the pilot is Friday, October 16, when Lesson 6.1 uses it.

3.4.2  What goes into a baseline: four families of reference values

2.4 minFigure 3.4.1 on screen. Go family by family with the Val-des-Pins example values; avoid drifting into Topic 4 detail.

Figure 3.4.1 groups the reference values of a baseline into four families, because each family is measured with a different part of the tool and answers a different question. Performance values describe how busy a system is: processor and memory use per hour, disk space and how fast it grows, the utilisation and delay of a network link. They come from the agent's inventory or from SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) counters on network devices, and they matter to monitoring for a reason you met in Class 4: a security problem often shows first as a performance change, such as a server that is suddenly busy at night. Network values describe who talks to whom: which hosts exchange traffic, over which ports and protocols, and how much per hour. For Val-des-Pins, "PC-ACCT-01 talks to SRV-FILE-01 and to the cloud mail service, and to nothing else" is a network reference value; so is "no SMB (Server Message Block) file-sharing traffic ever comes from the guest Wi-Fi".

Event values describe what the logs normally contain: how many successful and failed logons per hour and per account, how many errors per day, how many events each source produces per day. The last one, event volume per source, is the reference value that protects the envelope you computed in Class 7: FW-01 produces about 1,100 MB (Megabyte) of logs per day in the pilot, and a day at 3,000 MB (Megabyte) is itself an anomaly worth a look, whatever the content. Configuration and file values describe what a system is made of: the services that run, the ports that listen, the software installed with its versions, and the checksums of files that must not change silently. This last family is the FIM (File Integrity Monitoring) baseline: a table of file paths and their SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) values, the same function you used in 3.3 to verify a download. The Wazuh agent computes it during its first scan and re-checks it afterwards; the reference list is your responsibility, because only you know which files matter. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology, United States) SP (Special Publication) 800-128 (doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-128 VirusTotal check) calls the configuration part of this family the baseline configuration and treats it as the object that change management protects: a change is precisely a difference between the running configuration and the baseline configuration.

1.4 minEmphasize that every reference value carries metadata; without it the number is unusable.

Whatever the family, a reference value is never a bare number. It carries its source (which host or device), its metric (what exactly is counted, in which unit), its time bucket (which hours and days it applies to), the observation period it was measured over, the statistics that summarize it, and the administrative fields: who measured it, when, and which version of the baseline it belongs to. "Sixteen logons" is meaningless. "SRV-FILE-01, successful logons per hour, weekday 09:00, measured over ten weekdays from September 14 to 25, mean 15.2, standard deviation 1.7, baseline v1.0 approved September 28" is a reference value. 3.4.3  How to build one: observation period, buckets and statistics

1.8 minFigure 3.4.2 on screen. Steps 1 to 3 here, 4 and 5 in the next passage, 6 to 9 in 3.4.4.

Figure 3.4.2 lists the nine steps of the method; the same steps apply to a logon count, a bandwidth curve or a list of file hashes. Step one chooses the metric and the source from the monitoring plan of Lab 1: you do not baseline everything, you baseline what you decided to watch, in priority order. Step two fixes the observation period, also called the learning period: the span of time during which activity is recorded to be studied. The minimum is two full weeks, because most organizations live on a weekly cycle: a period shorter than a week never sees a weekend, and a single week has only one Monday, so nothing can be compared with anything. Longer is better when you can afford it; a month captures a month-end, a year captures seasons, but the pilot cannot wait a year. Step three is collection, and its rule is that nothing is changed on the system during collection: no new software, no new users, no changed schedules, otherwise the baseline describes a system that no longer exists.

2.6 minStatistics, slowly: mean, standard deviation, percentile. Use the 09:00 bucket numbers from the record. No formulas on screen beyond mean + 2 sd.

Step four groups the observations into time buckets: sets of hours that are expected to behave the same way. On SRV-FILE-01, nine in the morning on a Tuesday is comparable with nine in the morning on a Thursday, but not with three in the morning and not with Saturday. So the pilot uses one bucket per weekday hour of the day, twenty-four buckets that each collect ten values over the fourteen days, and one bucket for all weekend hours, because the server is idle at the weekend and one pooled bucket of ninety-six values is more reliable than forty-eight tiny ones. The choice of buckets is a decision you write down; a hospital would need different ones.

Step five computes the statistics of each bucket, and three of them are enough. The mean is the average of the values. The standard deviation, written with the Greek letter σ (sigma), measures how far the values usually spread around the mean: a small σ means the hour is predictable, a large σ means it varies a lot. If values follow a bell-shaped distribution, about 95 % of them fall within two standard deviations of the mean, and about 99.7 % within three, which is why "mean plus three σ" is the usual boundary of "normal". The 95th percentile, written p95, is the value below which 95 % of the observations fall; it is useful because it is not pulled up by a single extreme value the way the mean is. For the weekday 09:00 bucket of the pilot the numbers are: ten values, mean 15.2, σ 1.66, p95 17. Read that as: "on a weekday at nine, the file server sees about fifteen logons, rarely more than seventeen". One caution: an hour that is always zero has σ = 0, and "mean plus three σ" would then be zero too, so the pilot applies a floor of one to σ before computing any boundary. The two boundaries in the record, warning at mean plus two σ and alert at mean plus three σ, both rounded up, are the candidate thresholds that Lesson 3.5 will turn into alert rules on Saturday.

0.5 minRead the definitions once, slowly; students copy them.
Slide 43

Terms to learn

Baseline (reference database)
A documented description of the normal activity of a system, measured over a representative period, used as the comparison point for detection.
Observation (learning) period
The span of time during which activity is recorded to build the baseline; at least two full weekly cycles.
Time bucket
A set of hours expected to behave the same way (for example, weekday 09:00); statistics are computed per bucket.
Mean
The average of the values in a bucket.
Standard deviation (σ)
How far the values usually spread around the mean; small σ means predictable, large σ means variable.
95th percentile (p95)
The value below which 95 % of the observations in a bucket fall; not distorted by one extreme value.
Threshold
A boundary derived from the baseline (for example, mean + 3 σ) above which activity is treated as suspicious.

3.4.4  Cleaning, validating and documenting the baseline

2.2 minThe polluted baseline is the key risk. Use the contractor test: if kept, 35 logons at 22:00 become 'normal'.

Step six answers a question that beginners rarely ask: was the learning period itself normal? If an intruder, a contractor's test or a misconfigured backup was active during the two weeks, the baseline learns that activity as normal and will never alert on it again. This is called a polluted baseline, and it is the single most expensive mistake in this lesson, because it is invisible: the tool works, the numbers exist, and the alarm simply never rings. The defence is to test the learning data against itself before it is approved. For each hour, the pilot compares the value with the other values of its bucket, leaving the hour under test out of the comparison. Leaving it out matters: a value of 35 in a bucket whose other values are 0 and 1 would, if included, raise its own bucket's mean and σ so much that it would hide itself; this effect is called masking, and the leave-one-out comparison removes it. Any hour above the mean plus three σ of its peers is listed as suspicious.

Step seven is the owner review, and it is a conversation, not a calculation. The list of suspicious hours is shown to the person who knows the organization, at Val-des-Pins the owner and the part-time IT (Information Technology) contractor, and each hour receives a decision with a reason. In the pilot, three hours are flagged. Tuesday, September 22, at 22:00 and 23:00, with 35 and 20 logons: the contractor confirms a one-time migration test, documented in the change log, so both hours are excluded from the baseline. Friday, September 25, at 15:00, with 16 logons: a busy afternoon before a delivery, confirmed as ordinary, so the hour is kept. A statistical outlier is a question for the owner, not a conclusion. After the review the statistics are recomputed on the kept hours only: the weekday 22:00 bucket falls from a mean of 3.7 with σ 10.4 to a mean of 0.22 with σ 0.42, and its alert boundary from 36 logons to 4. The next migration test at ten in the evening will now be noticed.

1.8 minDocumentation and sign-off: version, owner, date, exclusions, review date. Link to Lab 2 and to 6.1.

Steps eight and nine turn the numbers into a Baseline Record. The record carries a baseline identifier with a version (BL-SRVFILE01-LOGONS-v1.0), the period, the number of observations kept and excluded with the reason for each exclusion, the bucket definition, the statistics per bucket, the candidate thresholds, and the administrative fields: who reviewed it, who approved it, on which date, and when it is reviewed next. The version number is not decoration. When the review of October 16 changes a threshold, the record becomes v1.1, and the alert rules of Lesson 3.5 point at a version, so that anyone can answer "which normal was this alert compared with?" Sign-off by the system owner is the last step: the owner confirms that the description of normal is acceptable to the organization, which also makes the owner accountable for the exclusions. The FIM (File Integrity Monitoring) part of the baseline follows the same path: a list of files with their SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) values, a date, and the rule that a difference is legitimate only when it corresponds to a change request.

Two practical warnings close the method. First, a baseline describes the pilot's own systems and nobody else's: section 7.2 of the Legal Notice reminds you that every baseline and log record is personal information about the people who used those systems, to be kept in the lab, kept to the minimum, and deleted when the exercise is marked. Second, a baseline is built from data the tool collected, never from what you believe the system does; if the collection shows that the backup service logs on at 02:00 every night, the baseline says so, even if the schedule document says 01:00, and the difference becomes a finding for Topic 5.

3.4.5  From baseline to thresholds: what Saturday's lesson needs from today

1.6 minShort bridge to 3.5 and Lab 2; show Figure 3.4.3 and read the 09:00 and 22:00 rows.

Lesson 3.5 tomorrow configures alerts for suspicious behaviours, and every alert rule needs a number to compare with. Figure 3.4.3 shows where those numbers come from: the teal bars are the mean of each weekday hour, the whiskers one standard deviation, the dashed amber line the warning boundary, the crimson line the alert boundary, and the two crimson dots the excluded hours of the contractor's test, drawn where they would have been. Read two rows of Table 3.4.3 and you have read the whole idea: weekday 09:00, mean 15.2, warning above 19, alert above 21; weekday 22:00, mean 0.22, warning above 3, alert above 4. The thresholds are called candidate thresholds because Lesson 3.5 will adjust them for the cost of a false alarm and the cost of a missed event, and Topic 6 will tune them again with real alert history. The baseline gives the starting point; without it, the starting point would be a guess.

Slides 51-52

Real-life example 3.4 - The first baseline of SRV-FILE-01

Task
Build the Baseline Record v1.0 of SRV-FILE-01 for the metric 'successful logons per hour' from a 14-day export, clean it after the owner review, derive the candidate thresholds, and add a file-integrity baseline of three critical files.
Relation to the lecture
This is the nine-step method of Figure 3.4.2 applied to the Tier 1 file server of Val-des-Pins, with the statistics of 3.4.3 and the cleaning of 3.4.4. It uses the data collected by the tool installed in the previous example and produces the numbers that Lesson 3.5 turns into alert rules.
Deliverable
The Baseline Record (Table 3.4.3, CSV (Comma-Separated Values)) and the file-integrity baseline (Table 3.4.4, CSV (Comma-Separated Values)) are Section 5 of the Lab 2 documentation. Because a lab cannot wait two weeks, the Lab 2 guide supplies a synthetic 14-day export like the one used here; the review of October 16 (Lab 3, Lesson 6.1) updates this record to v1.1.

The monitoring plan of Lab 1 lists SRV-FILE-01 as a Tier 1 asset and "successful logons per hour" as one of its watched metrics, because the shares it holds contain the accounting files and the drawings of the workshop. The export covers fourteen full days, Monday, September 14 to Sunday, September 27, 2026: 336 hourly counts. The shop works Monday to Friday from seven to five, so the weekday hours between 07:00 and 17:00 carry between five and sixteen logons on average, with a dip at noon; nights and weekends carry almost nothing, except one logon at 02:00 every day, which is the backup service copying the shares to NAS-01 and is expected. The buckets are the twenty-four weekday hours and one pooled weekend bucket.

The first statistics show something wrong in the evening: the weekday 22:00 bucket has a mean of 3.7 with a standard deviation of 10.4, which no ordinary evening produces. The leave-one-out test lists three suspicious hours: Tuesday, September 22 at 22:00 (35 logons) and 23:00 (20 logons), and Friday, September 25 at 15:00 (16 logons). You bring the list to the owner and the IT (Information Technology) contractor on Monday, September 28. The contractor recognizes the Tuesday evening at once: he ran a migration test on the shares that night, with a script that opened a session per folder, and it is written in the change log. Both hours are excluded with that reason. The Friday afternoon was a rush before a delivery, with everyone on the server at once; it is kept. The statistics are recomputed on 334 hours, and the 22:00 bucket returns to a mean of 0.22 with an alert boundary of 4 logons.

You write the record: identifier BL-SRVFILE01-LOGONS-v1.0, period, 334 kept and 2 excluded observations with the reason, the twenty-five buckets with their mean, σ, p95, warning and alert values, reviewed and approved on September 28, next review October 16. You add the FIM (File Integrity Monitoring) baseline: the hosts file, the nightly backup script and the share-permissions file, each with its SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) value and the rule that a change is legitimate only through a change request. Both tables go into Section 5 of the Lab 2 documentation, and tomorrow the warning and alert columns become the numbers inside the first alert rules.

Code example 3.4 - Baseline builder (Python program, mirrored step by step in the page)

Task
The program generates the 14-day export of hourly logon counts used in the example (the same numbers every time, thanks to a fixed seed), groups them into buckets, computes mean, standard deviation and p95, finds the suspicious hours with the leave-one-out test, applies the owner's decisions, derives the candidate thresholds, and writes the Baseline Record and the file-integrity baseline as CSV (Comma-Separated Values) files.
Relation to the lecture
The functions follow the nine steps of Figure 3.4.2: collect (step 3), bucket_of (step 4), stats and thresholds (step 5 and Lesson 3.5), find_outliers (step 6), owner_review (step 7), and the CSV (Comma-Separated Values) writing in main (steps 8 and 9). The visualization shows the export growing day by day, then the weekday profile with its statistics, the flagged hours, the cleaned profile and the thresholds.

34BUSINESS_PROFILE = {7: 6, 8: 14, 9: 16, 10: 13, 11: 12, 12: 8, 13: 12, 14: 13, 15: 12, 16: 10, 17: 5}
35# The names of the days, starting on Monday, used in the printed trace and the CSV.
