38# A fixed starting value makes the "random" numbers identical on every run and in the web version.
39_state = 20261002
40
41
42# A small linear congruential generator: same formula in Python and in the page's JavaScript.
43def rnd():
44 # The state is a global value that changes on every call.
45 global _state
46 # Multiply, add, and keep 31 bits: this is the classic generator formula.
47 _state = (1103515245 * _state + 12345) & 0x7FFFFFFF
48 # Divide by 2^31 to obtain a number between 0 and 1.
49 return _state / 2147483648.0
50
51
52# Produce one hour of synthetic activity around an expected value.
53def noisy(mean):
54 # Three uniform numbers added together give a bell-shaped noise between -1.5 and +1.5.
55 noise = (rnd() + rnd() + rnd()) - 1.5
56 # The noise is scaled with the square root of the mean, like counted events behave.
57 value = mean + noise * math.sqrt(max(mean, 1)) * 1.1
58 # Counts cannot be negative and must be whole numbers.
59 return max(0, round(value))
60
61
62# Step 1: build the 14-day export of hourly counts, including two known disturbances.
63def collect():
64 # The export is a list of dictionaries, one per hour.
65 rows = []
66 # Loop over every hour of the 14 days.
67 for h in range(PERIOD_DAYS * 24):
68 # Day number since the start (0 = Monday Sept 14) and the hour of the day.
69 day, hod = h // 24, h % 24
70 # Monday to Friday are weekdays; Saturday and Sunday are the weekend.
71 weekday = (day % 7) < 5
72 # Business hours on a weekday follow the expected profile.
73 if weekday and hod in BUSINESS_PROFILE:
74 count = noisy(BUSINESS_PROFILE[hod])
75 # Any other weekday hour is almost empty (an occasional late logon).
76 elif weekday:
77 count = 1 if rnd() < 0.15 else 0
78 # Weekend hours are quieter still.
79 else:
80 count = 1 if rnd() < 0.05 else 0
81 # The nightly backup service logs on every day at 02:00: this is normal and must stay.
82 if hod == 2:
83 count += 1
84 # Disturbance: a contractor ran a migration test on Tuesday Sept 22 late in the evening.
85 if day == 8 and hod == 22:
86 count = 35
87 # The same test continued into the next hour.
88 if day == 8 and hod == 23:
89 count = 20
90 # Store the hour with its labels; "keep" will be set to False for excluded hours.
91 rows.append({"day": day, "dow": DAYS[day % 7], "hod": hod, "weekday": weekday, "count": count, "keep": True})
92 # The whole export is returned to the caller.
93 return rows
94
95
96# Step 2: group the hours into buckets that share the same expected behaviour.
97def bucket_of(row):
98 # Weekday hours are compared with the same hour of other weekdays.
99 if row["weekday"]:
100 return f"weekday {row['hod']:02d}:00"
101 # All weekend hours are pooled because the server is essentially idle.
102 return "weekend (any hour)"
103
104
105# Step 3: compute mean, standard deviation and the 95th percentile of a list of counts.
106def stats(values):
107 # The number of observations in the bucket.
108 n = len(values)
109 # The mean is the sum divided by the count.
110 mean = sum(values) / n
111 # The variance is the average squared distance from the mean.
112 var = sum((v - mean) ** 2 for v in values) / n
113 # The standard deviation is the square root of the variance.
114 sd = math.sqrt(var)
115 # The 95th percentile is the value below which 95 % of observations fall.
116 p95 = sorted(values)[min(n - 1, int(math.ceil(0.95 * n)) - 1)]
117 # All four numbers are returned together.
118 return n, mean, sd, p95
119
120
121# Step 4: derive candidate thresholds from the statistics (used by Lesson 3.5).
122def thresholds(mean, sd):
123 # A floor of one keeps thresholds meaningful when a bucket never varies (sd = 0).
124 sd_eff = max(sd, 1.0)
125 # Warning at mean + 2 standard deviations, rounded up to a whole count.
126 warning = math.ceil(mean + 2 * sd_eff)
127 # Alert at mean + 3 standard deviations: statistically rare under normal activity.
128 alert = math.ceil(mean + 3 * sd_eff)
129 # Both values are returned.
130 return warning, alert
131
132
133# Step 5: compute the statistics of every bucket from the rows that are kept.
134def compute(rows):
135 # Collect the values of each bucket.
136 groups = {}
137 # Only kept rows enter the statistics.
138 for r in rows:
139 # A row that was excluded after the owner review is skipped.
140 if r["keep"]:
141 groups.setdefault(bucket_of(r), []).append(r["count"])
142 # The result maps a bucket name to its statistics.
143 return {b: stats(v) for b, v in groups.items()}
144
145
146# Step 6: find hours in the learning data that are far above the normal range of their bucket.
147def find_outliers(rows):
148 # Group the rows by bucket so each hour can be compared with its peers.
149 groups = {}
150 # Every row joins the list of its bucket.
151 for r in rows:
152 groups.setdefault(bucket_of(r), []).append(r)
153 # The outliers are collected in a list.
154 found = []
155 # Every hour is tested against the other hours of its bucket.
156 for r in rows:
157 # The hour under test is left out: otherwise a huge value inflates its own average and hides itself (masking).
158 others = [x["count"] for x in groups[bucket_of(r)] if x is not r]
159 # Statistics of the peers only.
160 n, mean, sd, p95 = stats(others)
161 # An hour is suspicious when it exceeds mean + 3 standard deviations of its peers (floor of 1).
162 if r["count"] > mean + 3 * max(sd, 1.0):
163 found.append(r)
164 # The suspicious hours are returned for the owner review.
165 return found
166
167
168# Step 7: the owner review decides, hour by hour, whether a suspicious value is normal.
169def owner_review(outliers):
170 # The decisions are printed so the class can see the reasoning.
171 for r in outliers:
172 # Tuesday Sept 22 late evening was the contractor's migration test: not normal activity.
173 if r["day"] == 8 and r["hod"] in (22, 23):
174 r["keep"] = False
175 decision = "EXCLUDE - contractor migration test, one-time, documented in change log"
176 # Anything else would be discussed individually; in this dataset nothing else is flagged.
177 else:
178 decision = "KEEP - confirmed normal by the owner"
179 # Print the decision.
180 print(f" review {r['dow']} day {r['day']+1:02d} {r['hod']:02d}:00 count={r['count']:>3} -> {decision}")
181
182
183# The main sequence follows the method of Lesson 3.4 from start to finish.
184def main():
185 # Announce what is being built.
186 print(f"Baseline for {SOURCE}: {METRIC}, period {PERIOD_START} + {PERIOD_DAYS} days")
187 # Step 1: collect (here: generate) the 14-day export.
188 rows = collect()
189 # Report the size of the learning data.
190 print(f"[1] collected {len(rows)} hourly observations")
191 # The raw export is saved so the class can open it in a spreadsheet.
192 with open("SRV-FILE-01_logons_14days.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
193 # A writer formats the rows.
194 w = csv.writer(f)
195 # Header of the raw export.
196 w.writerow(["day_no", "day", "hour", "successful_logons"])
197 # One line per hour.
198 w.writerows([[r["day"] + 1, r["dow"], f"{r['hod']:02d}:00", r["count"]] for r in rows])
199 # Steps 2 and 3: first statistics, computed on the raw data.
200 table = compute(rows)
201 # Report the number of buckets.
202 print(f"[2] {len(table)} buckets computed (24 weekday hours + 1 weekend bucket)")
203 # Step 6: find the hours that pollute the learning data.
204 outliers = find_outliers(rows)
205 # Report them.
206 print(f"[3] {len(outliers)} suspicious hours found in the learning data:")
207 # Step 7: owner review of each suspicious hour.
208 owner_review(outliers)
209 # Steps 2 and 3 again, without the excluded hours: the clean baseline.
210 table = compute(rows)
211 # Report the recalculation.
212 print(f"[4] statistics recomputed on {sum(1 for r in rows if r['keep'])} kept observations")
213 # Step 8: write the Baseline Record with header lines that identify the baseline.
214 with open("Table_3.4.3_Baseline_Record_SRV-FILE-01.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
215 # A writer formats the rows.
216 w = csv.writer(f)
217 # Identification lines: which baseline, which period, who owns it, when it is reviewed.
218 w.writerow(["baseline_id", "BL-SRVFILE01-LOGONS-v1.0", "source", SOURCE, "metric", METRIC])
219 w.writerow(["period", f"{PERIOD_START} + {PERIOD_DAYS} days", "excluded", "2 hours (Sept 22 22:00-23:59)", "next review", "2026-10-16 (Topic 6.1)"])
220 # Column names of the reference values.
221 w.writerow(["bucket", "n", "mean", "std_dev", "p95", "warning_threshold", "alert_threshold"])
222 # One row per bucket, in a readable order.
223 for b in sorted(table):
224 # Unpack the statistics.
225 n, mean, sd, p95 = table[b]
226 # Derive the candidate thresholds.
227 warning, alert = thresholds(mean, sd)
228 # Write the row with rounded values.
229 w.writerow([b, n, round(mean, 2), round(sd, 2), p95, warning, alert])
230 # Print a few key buckets so the trace stays short.
231 if b in ("weekday 02:00", "weekday 09:00", "weekday 22:00", "weekend (any hour)"):
232 print(f" {b:<20} n={n:<3} mean={mean:5.2f} sd={sd:4.2f} p95={p95:<3} warn>{warning:<3} alert>{alert}")
233 # Report the file.
234 print("[5] Baseline Record written -> Table_3.4.3_Baseline_Record_SRV-FILE-01.csv")
235 # Step 9: the file-integrity baseline: a reference hash for each file that must not change silently.
236 files = {
237 "C:\\Windows\\System32\\drivers\\etc\\hosts": "# hosts file of SRV-FILE-01 - managed by IT, last change 2026-08-30\n127.0.0.1 localhost\n",
238 "C:\\Scripts\\nightly-backup.ps1": "# Nightly backup to NAS-01 at 02:00 - service account svc-backup\nRobocopy D:\\Shares \\\\NAS-01\\backup /MIR /LOG:C:\\Logs\\backup.log\n",
239 "C:\\ProgramData\\VdP\\share-permissions.xml": "<shares><share name='Comptabilite' group='GRP-ACCT' rights='modify'/><share name='Atelier' group='GRP-SHOP' rights='read'/></shares>\n",
240 }
241 # The hashes are written to a second record.
242 with open("Table_3.4.4_FIM_Baseline_SRV-FILE-01.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
243 # A writer formats the rows.
244 w = csv.writer(f)
245 # Header of the file-integrity baseline.
246 w.writerow(["file", "sha256", "baseline_date", "expected_change"])
247 # One row per file with its reference SHA-256.
248 for path, content in files.items():
249 # The hash is computed on the file content (here, simulated content).
250 digest = hashlib.sha256(content.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
251 # Record the reference value and when a change would be legitimate.
252 w.writerow([path, digest, "2026-09-27", "only through a change request"])
253 # Print the shortened hash for the trace.
254 print(f" FIM {path:<45} {digest[:16]}...")
255 # Report the second file.
256 print("[6] File-integrity baseline written -> Table_3.4.4_FIM_Baseline_SRV-FILE-01.csv")
257 # Final reminder of what happens next in the course.
258 print("[7] Baseline v1.0 ready for sign-off; thresholds feed Lesson 3.5 (alerts); review scheduled Oct 16 (Lesson 6.1)")
259
260
261# Standard Python entry point.
262if __name__ == "__main__":
263 # Run the whole method.
264 main()
Download

Step-by-step explanation

  1. The program first fixes the metric, the source and the period, then defines the expected weekday profile from 07:00 to 17:00. A small pseudo-random generator with a fixed starting value produces the same 'random' counts every time, in Python and in the page, so that the numbers in the lecture, the tables and the simulator all agree.
  2. collect() builds 336 rows, one per hour, with the day of the week, the hour, a weekday flag and the count. It adds the backup logon at 02:00 every day, and injects the contractor's test on Tuesday evening (35 then 20 logons), so that the cleaning step has something real to find.
  3. bucket_of() gives each hour the name of its bucket: 'weekday 09:00' for weekday hours, 'weekend (any hour)' for all weekend hours. stats() computes the number of values, the mean, the standard deviation and the 95th percentile of a list; thresholds() derives warning (mean + 2 σ) and alert (mean + 3 σ), with a floor of 1 on σ, rounded up.
  4. compute() groups the kept rows by bucket and calls stats() on each group: 25 buckets, 24 with ten values and one with ninety-six.
  5. find_outliers() tests every hour against the other hours of its bucket, leaving itself out, so that a very large value cannot hide behind the average it inflated (masking). Three hours are returned.
  6. owner_review() applies the decisions of the review meeting: the two Tuesday evening hours are marked as not kept, with the reason printed; the Friday afternoon is kept. compute() is then run again on the kept rows only.
  7. main() writes the Baseline Record with two identification lines (identifier, source, metric, period, exclusions, next review) followed by one row per bucket, and prints four buckets so the trace stays readable. Then it hashes the content of three critical files with SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) and writes the file-integrity baseline.
  8. The last line of the trace states what happens next: v1.0 is ready for sign-off, the thresholds feed Lesson 3.5, and the review is scheduled for October 16 (Lesson 6.1). Both CSV (Comma-Separated Values) files are the Lab 2 deliverable in their final form.

0.8 minQuick recall: read each question, let a student answer, then flip.
Slide 57

Flash cards (click to flip)

Card 1What is a baseline (reference database)?click to flip
Answer 1A documented description of the normal activity of a system, measured over a representative period, stored with source, metric, bucket, period, statistics, date, owner and version, and used as the comparison point for detecting anomalies.click to flip back
Card 2Why must the observation period cover at least two full weeks?click to flip
Answer 2Because most organizations follow a weekly cycle: a shorter period never sees a weekend, and a single week has only one Monday, so nothing can be compared with anything.click to flip back
Card 3What is a time bucket, and why does the pilot use one bucket per weekday hour plus one weekend bucket?click to flip
Answer 3A set of hours expected to behave the same way. Nine in the morning on a Tuesday compares with nine on a Thursday, not with three in the morning or Saturday; the idle weekend is pooled into one bucket for reliability.click to flip back
Card 4What is a polluted baseline, and how is it prevented?click to flip
Answer 4A baseline that learned abnormal activity from the learning period as if it were normal, so it never alerts on it again. Prevented by testing each hour against its peers (leave-one-out) and by an owner review that excludes what was not normal.click to flip back
Card 5How are the candidate thresholds derived from a bucket's statistics?click to flip
Answer 5Warning = mean + 2 standard deviations, alert = mean + 3 standard deviations, with a floor of 1 on the standard deviation, rounded up; Lesson 3.5 adjusts them and Topic 6 tunes them.click to flip back

Slides 58-60

Self-check: 4 multiple-choice and 2 multiple-select questions

MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question): one correct option out of four. MSQ (Multiple-Select Question): six options, the number of correct ones is stated. Each question has a hint, a check, and an explanation for every option.

MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) - one answerQ7. SRV-FILE-01 shows 35 successful logons at 22:00 on a Tuesday. What decides whether this is an anomaly?
Hint: Think about what the tool needs before it can call anything abnormal.
AThe number 35 itself: more than 30 logons in an hour is always abnormal.
A number has no meaning on its own; 35 at 09:00 is ordinary on this server.
BThe comparison with the baseline value of the weekday 22:00 bucket and its threshold.
Correct. The baseline says what 22:00 normally looks like here (mean 0.22, alert above 4), so 35 is far outside it.
CThe type of server: file servers are never accessed at night.
Whether a file server is accessed at night depends on the organization; the backup logs on at 02:00 here.
DThe vendor's default rule set, which knows the normal values of every organization.
Default rules know signatures of known bad events, not what is normal in a woodworking shop in Laval.
MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) - one answerQ8. The weekday 03:00 bucket of SRV-FILE-01 has a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 0. What does the pilot do before computing the alert boundary?
Hint: Mean plus three times zero is zero.
ARemoves the bucket, because a bucket with no activity cannot be monitored.
An hour that is always empty is exactly where a logon should be noticed; the bucket is kept.
BApplies a floor of 1 to the standard deviation, so the alert boundary becomes 3 logons.
Correct. With σ floored at 1, warning = 0 + 2 = 2 and alert = 0 + 3 = 3: three logons at 03:00 raise an alert.
CMerges the 03:00 bucket with the 09:00 bucket to obtain a larger standard deviation.
Merging unlike hours destroys the meaning of the bucket; 03:00 must not be compared with 09:00.
DUses the 95th percentile of the 09:00 bucket instead.
The 09:00 statistics describe a different hour and would make 17 logons at 03:00 look normal.
MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) - one answerQ9. Why is each hour tested against the other hours of its bucket with itself left out (leave-one-out)?
Hint: Recall what a value of 35 does to the mean and standard deviation of nine values near zero.
ABecause the tool cannot compute statistics on ten values.
Ten values are enough for the pilot's statistics; the issue is not the count.
BBecause a very large value included in its own bucket inflates the mean and standard deviation enough to hide itself (masking).
Correct. Included, the 35 raised the 22:00 bucket's boundary to 36 and was not flagged; left out, it was flagged at once.
CBecause the hour under test belongs to a different day of the week.
All hours of a bucket are, by definition, comparable; the day of the week is already part of the bucket choice.
DBecause leaving one value out makes the mean equal to the 95th percentile.
Leaving one value out does not change what the percentile measures.
MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) - one answerQ10. Which of the following is a complete reference value, as the Baseline Record requires?
Hint: A reference value carries source, metric, bucket, period, statistics and administrative fields.
A"16 logons."
A bare number has no source, metric, bucket or period.
B"About 15 logons in the morning on the file server."
'About' and 'morning' are not a bucket or a statistic; nobody can compare against this.
C"SRV-FILE-01, successful logons per hour, weekday 09:00, Sept 14-25 (10 weekdays), mean 15.2, σ 1.66, p95 17, baseline v1.0 approved Sept 28."
Correct. Every field of Table 3.4.2 is present, so the value can be compared, versioned and reviewed.
D"SRV-FILE-01 is busy from 08:00 to 17:00."
A description of busy hours is useful context but not a reference value for a metric.
MSQ (Multiple-Select Question) - select 3Q11. Which three statements about the owner review are correct? (select 3)
Hint: The review is a conversation with reasons, and its outcome is not always 'exclude'.
AA statistical outlier is a question for the owner, not yet a conclusion.
Correct: the statistics flag, the owner decides.
BEvery flagged hour must be excluded, otherwise the baseline is polluted.
Flagged is not the same as abnormal; the Friday rush was kept.
CEach decision is recorded with its reason (for example, 'contractor migration test, documented in the change log').
Correct: reasons make the exclusions accountable and reviewable.
DThe Friday 15:00 rush before a delivery was kept because the owner confirmed it as ordinary activity.
Correct: this is exactly what happened in the pilot.
EThe review is done by the tool automatically from the vendor's rules.
The tool cannot know that a migration test took place; only people can.
FThe review is skipped when the learning period is longer than two weeks.
A longer period reduces the weight of one strange hour but never removes the need to look.
MSQ (Multiple-Select Question) - select 3Q12. Which three items must a Baseline Record contain for its numbers to be usable? (select 3)
Hint: Without these, nobody can answer 'which normal was this alert compared with?'
AA version number and the date of approval.
Correct: alert rules point at a version; reviews create the next one.
BThe observation period and the number of observations kept and excluded, with the reason for each exclusion.
Correct: the period and the exclusions say what 'normal' was built from.
CThe personal names of every employee whose logons were counted.
Counts per account may be a metric, but the record does not need names, and section 7.2 says to keep the minimum personal information.
DThe next review date.
Correct: a baseline drifts; the review date is set when it is created.
EA screenshot of the vendor's website.
Irrelevant to the reference values.
FThe password of the monitoring server's administrator account.
Never; credentials are confidential (section 17.2) and have no place in a record.

Lab 2 summary - Integrative Project, Part 2 (Saturday, October 3)

Slides 61-622.5 min
1.0 minSummary only: the Lab 2 guide is a separate document. Do not start the lab here.

Lab 2 is the second part of the Integrative Project (5 % of the final grade). It is assigned on Saturday, October 3 (Class 12), right after Lesson 3.5, and it asks each student to install and configure a monitoring tool on the Part 1 network, build the baseline, and set the alerts. The "Part 1 network" is the Val-des-Pins network you mapped in Lab 1, with your required variation. The tool is the one your Class 8 decision selected; the pilot in this lecture uses Wazuh on MON-01, but a student whose decision record selected the runner-up installs that one and documents the same stages.

0.9 minMap today's two deliverables to the Lab 2 sections; students should recognize them.

The Lab 2 documentation has six sections. Sections 1 to 3 are the Tool Selection Record from Class 8 (coverage map, decision matrix, decision record). Section 4 is the Installation and Update Record of today's Lesson 3.3 (Table 3.3.5 is the model). Section 5 is the Baseline Record and the file-integrity baseline of Lesson 3.4 (Tables 3.4.3 and 3.4.4 are the models; the guide supplies a synthetic 14-day export, because a lab cannot wait two weeks). Section 6, the alert rules, comes from Lesson 3.5 on Saturday. Lab 3 (October 16, Topic 6) reopens Sections 4 and 5 to update the baseline and propose optimizations.

Bring to Saturday's session: the lab VM (Virtual Machine) with a fresh snapshot, your Class 8 decision record, the Class 7 priority order, and the Lab 1 network map. Submission format, file names and the due date are stated in the Lab 2 guide and on the Léa DropBox; Lab 1 is due on Sunday, October 11, 23:59 EDT (Eastern Daylight Time).

Rules that apply to Lab 2. The signed Annex A acknowledgement must be on file before you touch the lab; the installation happens only inside your Authorized Lab Environment, isolated from any other network, with a snapshot taken first (section 6.4); every download comes from the official publisher and is checked (Annex C, section 14.2); every log, capture and baseline is fictional data kept in the lab and deleted after grading (sections 6.7, 7.2 and 18.2); course credentials, virtual machines and datasets are never shared or published (section 17.2). Wrap-up

Slides 63, 671.2 min
1.2 minClose with the three dates; thank them and stop on time.

What to keep from today. An installation is a procedure with seven stages, and the three most often skipped (preparing, verifying, recording) are the ones that make it trustworthy and repeatable. Updates come in three kinds, are applied in a fixed order (manager, agents, content), never without a way back, and always with a verification that triggers a rollback when it fails. A baseline is a documented, versioned description of normal activity, built over at least two weekly cycles, cleaned after an owner review, and turned into warning and alert thresholds that Saturday's lesson will put into the first alert rules.

Dates. Saturday, October 3: Lesson 3.5 (alerts) and Lab 2 start. Saturday, October 10: Quiz 3. Sunday, October 11, 23:59 EDT (Eastern Daylight Time): Lab 1 due on the Léa DropBox. Friday, October 16: Lab 3, where the baseline built today is reviewed and updated.
